newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Alestra wins ballot drive in Queretaro.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Alestra wins ballot drive in Queretaro.

text.p: Mexican telephone firm Alestra, backed by U.S. giant AT&T, won the majority of the pre-subscription ballots cast by residents in the central city of Queretaro, officials said on Tuesday.

Surprisingly to some, former monopoly Telefonos de Mexico (Telmex) was second in the voting to pick a long-distance carrier, said Carlos Casasus, head of the Federal Telecommunications Commission (Cofetel).
Alestra -- formed by AT&T, Mexican industrial firm Alfa and holding company and bank VISA-Bancomer -- obtained about 36.83 percent of the 19,151 ballots cast by city residents as of January 10.
Telmex won 34.44 percent of the ballots, Casasus said.
Avantel, a company formed by MCI Communications and Mexican bank Banacci, was in third place with 28.27 percent.
A handful of other firms won several dozen votes each, Casasus said.
Out of 77,187 telephone lines in Queretaro that are either business or residential, some 58,036 did not respond to the balloting process, Cofetel said in a separate statement.

Queretaro was the first Mexican city opened to telephone competition on January 1. The northern industrial city of Monterrey, Mexico's third largest, opened on January 10, but officials have not released information about the pre-subscription process there. By mid-year, the entire country will have competition in the telephone market.
The balloting process allows residents or businesses to select a long-distance carrier a month or two before their city opens to competition.
If residents do not return their ballots, they can still choose different carriers for each call by dialing a three-digit prefix. If they do not do either, the call automatically goes through Telmex.
Casasus told reporters he was pleased with the liberalization process in Mexico's market and said it had a more successful start than other countries that have opened their telecommunications market.
